faq.a: AST is present in red cells and muscle; malaria causes hemolysis and muscle breakdown, raising AST disproportionately.
faq.q: Why is AST often higher than ALT in malaria?

faq.a: No; early injury may have normal creatinine; look at urine output and urine microscopy.
faq.q: Can a normal creatinine rule out kidney injury?

faq.a: Give IV calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium before other measures.
faq.q: What is the first step when a patient has hyperkalaemia and a wide QRS?

exam: A patient with severe malaria presents with jaundice and a serum bilirubin of 180 µmol/L – what does this pattern suggest and how does it affect management? — Likely mixed hepatic and hemolytic jaundice; treat malaria urgently, monitor liver function, avoid hepatotoxic drugs.

You receive a BMP showing Na+ 128 mmol/L, K+ 6.2 mmol/L, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL in a dehydrated child with sickle‑cell disease – what are your priorities? — Correct hyperkalaemia first (calcium, insulin‑glucose), then rehydrate cautiously, assess for acute kidney injury.

A HIV‑positive patient on tenofovir has a rising creatinine and low phosphate – what is the likely cause and next step? — Tenofovir nephrotoxicity; stop drug, switch to alternative ART, monitor renal function.
How would you differentiate between SIADH and dehydration in a patient with hyponatraemia? — Assess volume status, urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg in SIADH), and urine Na+ (>30 mmol/L in SIADH).

A child with severe malnutrition has low calcium and phosphate – why are these values critical and how do you manage them? — Risk of refeeding syndrome; correct electrolytes slowly before nutrition, monitor for cardiac arrhythmias.

When is it acceptable to rely on bedside urine dipstick for proteinuria in a resource‑limited setting? — When quantitative protein measurement is unavailable and you need to screen for nephropathy; confirm with microscopy if possible.
Why should you avoid ACE inhibitors in a patient with hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury? — They reduce aldosterone‑mediated potassium excretion, worsening hyperkalaemia and renal perfusion.
A patient on herbal medicine presents with elevated transaminases – what steps do you take? — Take a detailed history of the herb, stop it, assess for viral hepatitis, and monitor liver enzymes.
ai.title: Blood Biochemistry
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Blood biochemistry tests reveal organ function, metabolic status and electrolyte balance. Clinicians interpret patterns to diagnose common tropical diseases and guide urgent care in low‑resource settings.

b: Key panels: basic metabolic panel (BMP), liver function tests (LFTs), renal profile, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, phosphate, bilirubin, enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, LDH, CK).
In low‑resource hospitals, point‑of‑care glucometers and handheld electrolyte meters are common; full panels may be sent to regional labs.
sections.p: Blood biochemistry measures small molecules, enzymes and electrolytes in plasma or serum. Results integrate liver, kidney, pancreas, muscle and endocrine function, and are essential for bedside decision‑making.

b: ALT/AST → hepatocyte injury; AST also in muscle, heart, RBCs.
Creatinine & urea → glomerular filtration; BUN rises with dehydration, high protein intake.
Electrolytes (Na+, K+, Cl−, HCO3−) → renal handling, acid‑base status, hormonal control.
sections.p: Enzymes leak from damaged cells; metabolites reflect production or clearance; electrolytes are regulated by kidneys, hormones and fluid shifts. Understanding source and clearance helps locate pathology.

b: Renal tubular reabsorption controls Na+ and K+; failure causes hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia.
Insulin drives glucose into cells; lack leads to hyperglycaemia.
sections.p: Homeostatic mechanisms maintain narrow ranges: renal excretion, hormonal feedback (aldosterone, ADH, parathyroid hormone), hepatic metabolism and cellular uptake.

b: Elevated ALT/AST with high bilirubin → viral hepatitis, malaria‑induced hepatic injury, herbal toxin.
Rising creatinine + low urine output → acute kidney injury from severe malaria, sepsis, or nephrotoxic drugs.
Hyperkalaemia in sickle‑cell crisis → renal tubular damage, hemolysis.
sections.p: Abnormal patterns point to organ injury, infection, malnutrition or drug toxicity. In tropical settings, malaria, hepatitis B, HIV‑associated nephropathy and sickle‑cell crises are frequent culprits.

b: Low Na+ with euvolemia → consider SIADH from TB meningitis.
High AST > ALT in malaria → muscle breakdown, not primary liver disease.
Elevated LDH with anaemia → hemolysis from sickle‑cell or malaria.
sections.p: Interpretation guides immediate management: fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, drug dosing, and referral. Recognising patterns prevents misdiagnosis when imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Is renal filtration impaired? – A rise > 1.5 mg/dL suggests acute kidney injury; if unavailable, use urine output and bedside ultrasound for kidney size.
Is there hepatocellular injury? – ALT > 40 U/L and AST > 40 U/L indicate injury; AST > ALT suggests muscle or hemolysis.
What is the acid‑base/electrolyte status? – Na+ < 135 mmol/L = hyponatraemia; K+ > 5.5 mmol/L = hyperkalaemia, needing urgent treatment.
Is the patient hypoglycaemic or hyperglycaemic? – Glucose < 3.0 mmol/L requires dextrose; > 11 mmol/L may need insulin.
Is jaundice due to hepatic or hemolytic cause? – Direct > 20 µmol/L points to cholestasis; indirect predominance suggests hemolysis or malaria.

b: Acute kidney injury – stop nephrotoxins, give IV fluids guided by urine output; consider dialysis if creatinine > 5 mg/dL and refractory hyperkalaemia.
Hyperkalaemia – give calcium gluconate (if ECG changes), insulin‑glucose, and consider loop diuretics; avoid potassium‑sparing drugs.
Severe hyponatraemia – raise Na+ slowly with hypertonic saline if symptomatic; avoid rapid correction to prevent osmotic demyelination.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct deranged biochemistry.

b: Elevated AST in malaria vs. alcoholic liver disease – check GGT and history of alcohol.
Low Na+ from dehydration vs. SIADH – assess volume status and urine osmolality.
sections.p: Distinguish biochemical patterns from similar‑appearing conditions.

b: Hemolysis in the sample raises AST, LDH, and potassium falsely.
Bilirubin may be spuriously low if the sample is delayed and bilirubin degrades.
sections.p: Be aware of factors that alter values independent of disease.

b: Link a single abnormal result to a pathophysiological mechanism.
Prioritise investigations when resources are limited.
Explain why a drug (e.g., ACE inhibitor) is avoided in hyperkalaemia.
